# Transcript data

Drop Lenny's Podcast transcripts here as plain `.txt` or `.md` files, one file
per episode. The filename (without extension) is used as the episode label
shown in citations, e.g. `ep-142-casey-winters-growth-loops.txt` becomes the
episode label `ep-142-casey-winters-growth-loops`.

## Where to get transcripts

Lenny's Podcast does not publish a bulk transcript API. Practical options:

1. **Manual export**: Lenny's newsletter posts include full transcripts for many
   episodes (lennysnewsletter.com) — copy/paste into a `.txt` file per episode.
2. **YouTube captions**: most episodes are on YouTube with auto-captions;
   download via `yt-dlp --write-auto-sub --skip-download <url>` and convert
   the `.vtt` to plain text.
3. **Podcast transcription service**: run episode audio through a
   transcription tool (e.g. Whisper) if you have the audio files.

This repo ships with 2 short SAMPLE transcripts (`sample-*.txt`) so the
ingestion pipeline and RAG flow can be demoed end-to-end without needing the
full corpus. Replace them with real transcripts for a production-quality demo.

## Running ingestion

```
cd backend
python -m app.ingestion.ingest_transcripts
```

This chunks every file here, embeds the chunks, and writes a FAISS index to
`FAISS_INDEX_DIR` (default `./data/faiss_index`). Re-run any time you add or
update transcripts — the index is fully rebuilt each run (see
`ingest_transcripts.py` docstring for why a full rebuild was chosen over
incremental updates at this corpus size).

Episode: Sample Episode - Fixing Onboarding and Activation

Host: Let's talk activation. How do you define it?

Guest: Activation is the first moment a new user experiences the core value
of the product, not just the first login. Teams often conflate "signed up"
with "activated," which hides a huge amount of drop-off in between.

Host: How do you find the right activation metric?

Guest: Look at retained users from six months ago and work backward: what
action did nearly all of them take in their first session that non-retained
users didn't take? That action, done within a specific time window, is your
activation event. It's an empirical exercise, not something you guess from a
whiteboard.

Host: What's a common onboarding mistake?

Guest: Front-loading configuration before the user has seen any value. Asking
someone to set up integrations, invite teammates, and customize settings
before they've experienced a single "aha moment" kills momentum. Get them to
value first, then ask for the setup work once they're bought in.

Host: How do you balance activation speed with import quality, like when a
user needs to connect real data?

Guest: Offer a sample-data path alongside the real-data path. Let users
explore with realistic sample data immediately, and let real data import run
in the background or as a secondary step. That way time-to-value isn't
gated on a slow or error-prone import process.

Episode: Sample Episode - Pricing Product-Led Growth Products

Host: Today we're talking about pricing strategy for product-led growth (PLG)
companies. What's the biggest mistake you see teams make?

Guest: The most common mistake is pricing based on what competitors charge
instead of pricing based on the value delivered to a specific user segment.
Teams copy a competitor's tiered pricing page without understanding why that
structure exists for the competitor's business model.

Host: How should a team think about their first pricing page instead?

Guest: Start by identifying your core value metric -- the thing that scales
with the value a customer gets, like seats, usage volume, or API calls. Then
build tiers around natural upgrade triggers tied to that metric, not around
arbitrary feature bundling. A generous free tier is a growth lever, not a
cost center, as long as the value metric creates a believable upgrade path.

Host: When should a team introduce usage-based pricing?

Guest: Usage-based pricing works best when the product has a metered resource
that customers can directly observe and control, and when adoption is
land-and-expand rather than a single big purchase decision. It's risky to
introduce too early, before you understand your own cost structure, because
you can end up subsidizing your heaviest users.

Host: Any advice on communicating a pricing change to existing users?

Guest: Grandfather existing customers wherever possible, over-communicate the
"why" behind the change in terms of value delivered, and give at least 30-60
days notice. Pricing changes that feel like a bait-and-switch are one of the
fastest ways to spike churn and hurt word-of-mouth growth.
